screens.h: Current is charge on the move
p: **Current** is the rate of flow of charge: **I = q/t**. The unit is the ampere: 1 A = 1 C·s⁻¹.
The battery does not make charge. It does **work** on charge that is already in every wire. The bulb transfers that energy to heat and light.

rules: Current is the **rate of flow of charge**: I = q/t.
A₁ and A₂ read the **same**: current is not used up.
Conventional current leaves the **+ terminal** (the long plate).

screens.q: A₁ and A₂ are on either side of the bulb, and A₁ reads 0,30 A. What does A₂ read?
choices: Lerato: A₂ reads less than A₁, because the bulb uses up some of the current.
The bulb transfers energy, not charge. Charge is not used up.
Zoe: A₂ reads the same as A₁. The bulb transfers energy, not charge.
The same charge passes A₁ and A₂ each second.
Ravi: A₁ reads more, because the current reaches it first.
The whole loop starts moving at the same instant, so A₁ is not “first”.
screens.why: Zoe ✓. The same charge passes A₁ and A₂ each second, and the whole loop starts moving at the same instant, like a rope loop pulled round.

An **ammeter** goes in series. A **voltmeter** goes across a component, in parallel.

rules: The **ammeter** is in series, with a resistance of about 0 Ω.
The **voltmeter** is across the bulb, in parallel, with a very high resistance.
The reading is the pd **between the two contact points**.

screens.q: Which sentence is the SAGS definition of potential difference?
choices: Potential difference is the work done per unit positive charge.
Potential difference is the work done per charge.
The word *positive* is missing. Without it, the definition is not the SAGS one.
Potential difference is the voltage at a point.
A single point has no pd. A pd is always *across* a component or *between* two points.
screens.why: “Definitions must be learnt strictly as they are in the SAGs.” (IEB Examiners’ Report 2022)

screens.h: In series, the pds add up
p: A voltmeter goes across one component and reads the pd across it.
In series, the pds across the components **add up to the battery’s pd**: V₁ + V₂ = 12 V.
The larger resistor takes the larger share of the pd.

screens.q: In the circuit above, V₁ across the 4 Ω reads 4 V. What does V₂ across the 8 Ω read?

traps: That is the battery’s pd. V₂ is across the 8 Ω only, and the 4 Ω takes 4 V of the 12 V.
That is V₁. The pds add up to 12 V, so V₂ = 12 − 4.
The pds add up to the battery’s 12 V: V₂ = 12 − 4.
num.hint: The pds add up to the battery’s pd: V₁ + V₂ = 12 V.

screens.why: V₁ + V₂ = 12 V, so V₂ = 12 − 4 = 8 V. Check with V = IR: I = 12/12 = 1 A, so V₂ = (1)(8) = 8 V.

screens.q: A torch bulb is connected to a battery. The pd across the bulb is 3 V and the current in the bulb is 0,5 A. (a) Define potential difference. (2) (b) Calculate the charge that passes through the bulb in 10 minutes. (3) (c) Calculate the energy transferred in the bulb by this charge. (3)

lines.x: Potential difference is the work done ✓ per unit positive charge ✓.

why: Each coulomb transfers 3 J in the bulb (V = W/q), so 300 C transfer 300 × 3 = 900 J.
